analysis.one_liner: Expands unpaid family leave to cover domestic partners and doubles leave for same-employer couples.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee in 2005 with no cosponsors and never came to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Family and Medical Leave Act in three ways: let workers certify a medical need with a nurse practitioner, not only a doctor; let workers take leave to care for a registered domestic partner, not only a legal spouse; and doubled the unpaid leave cap from 12 to 24 weeks for married couples or partners who work for the same employer. It never left the House subcommittee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers without a legal marriage certificate—domestic and civil partners—gain protected leave to care for a partner during a medical crisis. Workers in areas or situations without easy doctor access gain by using nurse practitioners to certify leave. Married or partnered couples who share an employer gain up to 24 weeks of combined protected leave instead of 12, doubling the time they can spend caring for a new child or ailing family member without losing their job.

how_it_helps.text: Adds registered domestic and civil partners to the FMLA's definition of spouse, so workers can take protected leave to care for a partner the law previously ignored.
Adds nurse practitioners to the list of health care providers whose certification supports FMLA leave, giving workers a more accessible certification option.
Extends the combined leave cap from 12 to 24 workweeks for spouses employed by the same employer.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers bear the cost of holding jobs open up to twice as long for same-employer couples and of processing more leave requests, all as unpaid leave; the public pays nothing directly.

drawbacks.text: The 24-week cap for same-employer couples doubles the maximum time one employer must hold two jobs open, a real cost for small businesses with limited staff.
All FMLA leave is unpaid, so the expansion helps workers keep jobs but does nothing to help them pay bills during the leave; a longer protected absence may strain workers financially.
The bill received no cosponsors, indicating little appetite in the House even among members who might support leave expansion generally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The expansion is modest and targeted: it reaches workers the 1993 law left out (domestic partners) and relieves a genuine certification bottleneck (nurse practitioners). The main cost falls on employers, mostly small ones, who must hold more jobs open longer, though the leave remains unpaid. A fair reading is that the benefits to a narrow group of workers outweigh the added burden, but the bill would not have transformed family leave for most Americans.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees, sent to a subcommittee a month later, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Juanita Millender-McDonald introduced the bill on January 6, 2005, the first session of the 109th Congress.
It was referred to the Committees on Education and the Workforce, House Administration, and Government Reform.
On February 9, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections of the Education and Workforce Committee.
No further action was taken; the bill had zero cosponsors and expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have had to hold jobs open for up to 24 weeks for same-employer couples are better off, and the FMLA's narrower coverage of spouses and physician-only certifications remained unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, whose FMLA obligations stay as-is

for.name: Rep. Juanita Millender-McDonald
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 6, 2005 and pursued no recorded follow-up action.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of primary referral, chaired by Rep. John Boehner (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to its Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on February 9, 2005, where it sat without a hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after receiving the referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and no vote was ever taken, so no party split is observable in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have required covered employers to hold jobs open up to twice as long for same-employer couples and to accept nurse-practitioner certifications and partner caregiving leave. That cost is the mirror of the protection workers would gain.
Their certifications would have counted for FMLA leave for the first time, giving them a formal role in a process currently reserved for physicians.
